description: Four-panel optical micrograph (OM) set of as-cast Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–xBe low-density steel, each panel carrying a panel letter in the top-left corner and a white-boxed 50 µm scale bar at the bottom right. (a) 0Be: a uniform, essentially single-phase austenite matrix with wavy light/dark dendritic (cellular) etching contrast; one red arrow marks the matrix as γ. (b) 0.5Be: the same cellular/dendritic matrix is now outlined by dark, point-like precipitates labelled "Beryllium compound" (yellow text with a pale-pink arrow); a red arrow again marks γ. (c) 1.0Be and (d) 1.5Be: the structure becomes clearly dual-phase, with large bright blocky/vermiform islands labelled δ (blue letter, navy arrow) embedded in a darker matrix labelled γ (red letter, dark-red arrow), and dark inter-island regions flagged by pale-pink arrows and the yellow "Beryllium compound" label. In (d) the bright δ islands appear finer and more fragmented than in (c). No magnification or composition values are printed on the panels beyond the 50 µm scale bars.

subfigures.description: OM of as-cast 0Be steel: a single, uniform austenite matrix with wavy light/dark cellular-dendritic etching contrast and scattered fine dark dots; one red arrow labels the matrix γ; 50 µm scale bar.

OM of as-cast 0.5Be steel: cellular/dendritic austenite matrix whose cell boundaries are decorated with dark point-like precipitates; yellow text 'Beryllium compound' with a pale-pink arrow points at these precipitates, a red arrow labels the matrix γ; 50 µm scale bar.

OM of as-cast 1.0Be steel: clearly dual-phase structure with large bright blocky/vermiform islands labelled δ (blue letter, navy arrow) in a darker matrix labelled γ (red letter, dark-red arrow), and dark inter-island regions labelled 'Beryllium compound' (yellow text, pale-pink arrows); 50 µm scale bar.

OM of as-cast 1.5Be steel: same dual-phase bright-δ-island / darker-γ-matrix structure as (c) but the bright islands appear finer, more fragmented and separated by a more continuous dark 'Beryllium compound' network; 50 µm scale bar.

observations.observation: All four panels are optical micrographs of the same magnification class, each with a white-boxed 50 µm scale bar and a top-left panel letter (a)-(d).
Panel (a), printed as 0Be, shows a uniform single-phase matrix with wavy light/dark cellular-dendritic etching contrast and only rare tiny dark dots.
Panel (b), printed as 0.5Be, shows dark point-like precipitates decorating the cell/dendrite boundaries; the yellow label 'Beryllium compound' with a pale-pink arrow identifies these dark points.
Panels (c) and (d), printed as 1.0Be and 1.5Be, show a distinctly two-phase structure of bright blocky/vermiform islands labelled δ against a darker matrix labelled γ.
In (d) the bright δ islands are visibly finer and more fragmented than the coarser bright islands in (c).
The figure caption identifies the panels as OM of as-cast Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–xBe low-density steel strips with (a) 0Be, (b) 0.5Be, (c) 1.0Be and (d) 1.5Be.
The citing text states that the microstructure of the beryllium-free steel (Fig. 2a) is completely austenitic.
The citing text states that at 0.5Be, black point compounds start to appear and attach to the austenite matrix, attributed to compounds produced after beryllium alloying.
The citing text states that when Be content exceeds about 0.5 wt%, a cross-like compound resembling an ancient Chinese character appears in the matrix and is known as the Be–Fe phase compound.

The citing text states that the Be precipitates appear at the boundary between austenite and ferrite, crossing vertically and horizontally like characters, and that Be addition also produces many spherical, rod-like or needle-like compounds.

The citing text states that in 1.0Be and 1.5Be steel much ferrite appears in the austenite matrix, consistent with the XRD results, and that the ferrite grain size of 1.5Be is evidently smaller than that of 1.0Be.
The citing text reports that increasing the Be–Fe phase content encroaches on the austenite matrix positions, decreasing both austenite and ferrite content in the higher-Be steels.
No numeric phase fractions, grain sizes or magnification values are printed on any panel; the only quantitative anchor visible in the pixels is the 50 µm scale bar.
